meta.title: Who really said "If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts he shall end in certainties"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely Francis Bacon, from The Advancement of Learning (1605), First Book, section V.8. The exact wording is in the original English text.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1561–1626 · English philosopher, statesman & father of the scientific method
answer.sourceLine: Written by Bacon in ‘The Advancement of Learning’ (1605), First Book, section V.8. The popular wording matches the original English text word-for-word — it is one of Bacon’s genuine lines, not a later paraphrase.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: For the two ways of contemplation are not unlike the two ways of action commonly spoken of by the ancients: the one plain and smooth in the beginning, and in the end impassable; the other rough and troublesome in the entrance, but after a while fair and even. So it is in contemplation: if a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.
trail: The line sits in the sourced section of Bacon’s Wikiquote page, cited to ‘The Advancement of Learning’ (1605), Book I, v, 8.
The exact sentence appears in the primary text on Project Gutenberg’s 1605 edition, in the section beginning “the two ways of contemplation”.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum holds a 20th-century ‘Great Ideas’ advertising print of the line, credited to Bacon and ‘The Advancement of Learning’ — though it uses the variant “end with doubts”.
source.excerptNote: Bacon is criticising “an impatience of doubt, and haste to assertion” — the line is his case for beginning inquiry in humility rather than false confidence.

source.rightsNote: ‘The Advancement of Learning’ was first published in 1605 and is long in the public domain in the United States; Bacon died in 1626. The original English text quoted here carries no subsisting copyright.

author.name: Francis Bacon
author.heading: About Francis Bacon
author.metaLine: 1561–1626 · English philosopher, statesman & pioneer of the scientific method
author.bio: Francis Bacon, 1st Viscount St Alban, was an English philosopher and statesman who served as Lord Chancellor under James I. He is remembered as a founder of empiricism and the inductive, experimental method — ideas he set out in ‘The Advancement of Learning’ (1605) and the ‘Novum Organum’ (1620). This line captures his core conviction that genuine knowledge grows from patient doubt rather than premature certainty.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is the rare feel-good line that is genuinely by the famous name attached to it. The confusion is not about who but about exact words and translation.

items.why: A common slip swaps “end in doubts” for “end with doubts.” Even the Smithsonian’s ‘Great Ideas’ print uses “end with doubts”; Bacon’s 1605 text reads “end in doubts.”

A shorter first-person form (“if we begin with certainties, we shall end in doubts”) also circulates widely — the Online Library of Liberty, for instance, renders it in the first person while still citing ‘The Advancement of Learning’ (1605). Bacon’s original 1605 English, though, is the third-person “if a man will begin…”.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound: the exact popular wording is Bacon’s own, in ‘The Advancement of Learning’ (1605), First Book, section V.8, per Wikiquote’s sourced section and the primary text.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Bacon wrote ‘The Advancement of Learning’ as a manifesto for a new, evidence-driven way of pursuing knowledge, dedicated to King James I. The line about certainties and doubts is a compact statement of his whole programme: that dogmatic confidence is a dead end, while disciplined, patient doubt is the road to real understanding.

It became a touchstone for the scientific method — the idea that inquiry should start by questioning, not by assuming — and it still surfaces wherever people argue for intellectual humility over premature certainty.
